title: How your ears hear
examples: How does sound actually get into my ear?
What is the job of the tiny bones in my ear?
Which part of the ear helps me keep my balance?

explain.say: Sound travels to us in waves through the air.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: the human ear. Look at the outer ear, the ear canal and the eardrum. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
These waves hit your eardrum and make it vibrate.
Three tiny bones then move to make the vibrations bigger.
Next, the vibrations go into the cochlea to be changed to signals.
Your inner ear also has parts that help your brain know your balance.
When you ride a swing, the movement tells your balance system you are moving.

faq.q: How do sound waves get turned into messages for my brain?
faq.a: The cochlea contains fluid that moves when the bones vibrate. This movement stimulates nerve endings that send electrical signals to your brain.
asks: How is sound converted to a signal?

faq.q: Are the three small bones in my ear really tiny?
faq.a: Yes, they are the smallest bones in the human body. They work together to make the vibrations stronger before they reach the inner ear.
asks: What is the job of the middle ear bones?
Why do I have three bones in my ear?

faq.q: If I spin around very fast, how does my body know to stop?
faq.a: Your inner ear has canals that detect movement in all directions. They send information about your head's position to your brain for balance.
asks: What part helps me keep my balance?
How does my body sense motion?

faq.q: Does the eardrum break if I get too much noise?
faq.a: Very loud sounds can damage the eardrum or the delicate structures inside the ear. It is important to protect your ears from loud noises.
asks: Can loud noises hurt my ears?
What is the danger of loud sounds?

faq.q: Do the bones help with balance too?
faq.a: No, the bones mainly help with hearing by amplifying sound vibrations. Balance is managed by separate structures in the inner ear.
asks: Are the bones for hearing or balance?
Which part handles the sense of balance?

facts: Sound travels through vibrations in a medium like air or water.
The eardrum vibrates when sound waves hit it.
The three tiny bones amplify these vibrations for efficiency.
The cochlea converts these vibrations into electrical nerve signals.

quiz.say: What is the first structure to vibrate when sound waves arrive?
quiz.why: The eardrum is the barrier that vibrates when sound waves hit it first.

wrong.0: The cochlea is further inside and handles the signals, not the initial vibration.
wrong.1: The tiny bones move after the eardrum vibrates to strengthen the sound.
wrong.2: The balance system deals with movement, not the initial sound reception.

quiz.say: If the tiny bones did not exist, what would happen to the sound signal?

options.show: You would lose your sense of balance.
options.say: You would lose your sense of balance.

quiz.why: The bones act like a lever system to make the vibrations stronger for the inner ear.

wrong.0: Speed is not the main issue; the signal strength is reduced without amplification.
wrong.1: The cochlea can still work, but the input signal would be too weak to process.
wrong.2: Hearing and balance are separate systems, so losing the bones affects hearing mainly.

quiz.say: When you turn your head quickly, which system sends signals to your brain?
quiz.why: The balance system, located in the inner ear, detects head movement and position.

wrong.0: The bones are part of the hearing mechanism, not the balance mechanism.
wrong.1: The cochlea is specialized for interpreting sound frequency, not head position.
wrong.3: The eardrum only responds to pressure waves, not rotational movement.
